title: Graph Fundamentals: Reachable Neighbors
contract: Given n vertices and undirected edges, return the sorted neighbors of source. Duplicate edges collapse; vertices are 0 through n−1.
brute: boolean[][] matrix=new boolean[n][n];for(int[] edge:edges){matrix[edge[0]][edge[1]]=true;matrix[edge[1]][edge[0]]=true;emit("Fill symmetric adjacency cells","edge",edge);}List<Integer> out=new ArrayList<>();for(int v=0;v<n;v++)if(matrix[source][v])out.add(v);return out;
optimal: List<Set<Integer>> graph=new ArrayList<>();for(int i=0;i<n;i++)graph.add(new TreeSet<>());for(int[] edge:edges){graph.get(edge[0]).add(edge[1]);graph.get(edge[1]).add(edge[0]);emit("Store only existing neighbor links","edge",edge,"source neighbors",graph.get(source));}return new ArrayList<>(graph.get(source));
reasoning: An adjacency matrix reserves one boolean for every possible pair, even for a sparse graph.
Adjacency sets store only present edges; adding both directions represents an undirected graph.

This sorted-set variant also removes duplicates. Lists offer O(V+E) construction if duplicates and ordering are handled separately; matrices can be preferable for dense graphs or constant-time edge queries.
complexity: O(V+E log V), O(V+E) for sorted sets
